findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the handler returns
findings.body: All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine and build the goroutine's context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the inbound apiserver request context. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which typically happens before/while the goroutine runs. The legacy store call therefore receives an already-cancelled context and its DB work will be aborted, so the "safe measure" legacy write silently never happens for most requests, leaving legacy storage permanently out of sync. The goroutine must detach from the request context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying only the needed values) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Legacy write errors in goroutines are swallowed with no logging
findings.body: In Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only used as a boolean for the duration metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since the caller has already received a success response, a failed legacy write now produces no error, no log line and no retry — divergence between unified and legacy storage becomes undiagnosable. Log the error (with name/kind) in each goroutine.

findings.title: Goroutines have no panic recovery; a legacy store panic crashes the process
findings.body: The four goroutines spawned in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Synchronous calls were previously protected by the apiserver's per-request panic handler; a panic on a bare goroutine terminates the whole Grafana process. Any panic in a legacy store (e.g. nil map/SQL layer bug) is now fatal instead of a 500 for one request. Add recovery (and log) around the goroutine body.

findings.title: Delete records object name in the `kind` metric label, causing unbounded cardinality
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This creates one Prometheus label value per deleted object name, producing unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics registry (memory growth / scrape bloat) and making the storage-duration metric unusable for deletes. It should be `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Create failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. No legacy call happened, so the legacy error/duration metric is polluted with storage failures and the storage failure itself is never recorded in the storage metric. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: Update failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error
findings.body: On `d.Storage.Update` failure the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, but the failing call was the unified storage one and no legacy call was made. The legacy error metric is inflated with storage errors and storage failures are not counted, which will make the dual-writer dashboards misattribute failures. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: DeleteCollection's legacy call records a storage-duration metric
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is reported via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy delete-collection latency/errors are therefore never visible in the legacy metric, and the storage metric double-counts with a legacy duration, skewing both series.

findings.title: Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object produced by unified storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy storage persisted exactly the object unified storage had written. Now the original `objInfo` is replayed against the legacy store. For PATCH/apply requests the transformation is recomputed against the legacy copy, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion precondition the version comes from unified storage, which does not match the legacy row's version — legacy updates will fail with conflicts or write a different object than unified storage, silently diverging the two stores.

findings.title: Object passed to the async legacy Create may be mutated concurrently with response serialization
findings.body: `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs on a goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was handed to `d.Storage.Create`. The generic registry store mutates the input object in place (name generation, resourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp) and typically returns that same pointer as `created`, which the apiserver serializes into the HTTP response after this function returns. The legacy store also mutates the object it is given. Two goroutines therefore read/write the same object without synchronization — a genuine data race that can corrupt the response body or the persisted legacy record. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine.

findings.title: Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write
findings.body: Every mode-3 write test (Create line 63, Delete line 228, DeleteCollection line 282, Update line 343) returns as soon as the dual writer returns, with no synchronization on the goroutine that performs the legacy write and no assertion that the legacy store was called. The core behaviour this PR introduces — "write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy" — is untested; the context-cancellation bug above would not be caught. In addition, because legacy and storage share a single `mock.Mock`, a legacy call cannot be distinguished from a storage call, and the goroutine can still be running (touching the mock) after the subtest finishes, which can race with test teardown. Use separate mocks per store plus a channel/WaitGroup (or `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting) to assert the legacy call happened.

findings.title: Delete stores the wrong logger in the context
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` puts the bare base logger into the context instead of `log`, which was just built with name/kind/method values. Downstream code that pulls the logger from the context loses all the request-scoped fields, unlike every other method in this file which passes `log`.

findings.title: go.work.sum gains a duplicate entry and unrelated dependency hashes
findings.body: The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...`, which already exists a couple of lines above, and adds hashes for modules (azure sdk, prometheus-alertmanager, old otel sdk/metric v0.39.0, otlp protos) that are unrelated to this change. This looks like an accidental/mechanical `go work sync` from a different module set; it makes the dual-writer PR carry unrelated dependency churn and the duplicate line will keep reappearing/disappearing in future diffs. Revert go.work.sum unless the change is actually required to build.

findings.title: Misleading List test case name
findings.body: The case is named "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" but mode 3 List is now implemented and the case simply asserts that a store error is propagated. The stale name (copied from the previous not-implemented behaviour) will confuse readers about what is covered.
